\section[\hi{दिन}]{\hi{दिन} (din) — "day," the same root as diēs, a different branch}

\label{lesson:HI-C25-din}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You've already met this word once, tucked inside \emph{dopahar} ("noon," literally "two pahars" of the \textbf{day}). Now it stands alone — and its connection to Latin's \emph{diēs} is real, but more careful than it first looks.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{दिन} — "day"}
\textbf{\hi{दिन}} (\textbf{din}) — "\textbf{day}" — is the ordinary Hindi word for "day," already implicit in \textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} (\emph{dopahar}, "noon," Chapter 17).

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The same ultimate root as diēs — but a separate branch}
\textbf{Din} traces to \textbf{Sanskrit} \textbf{\hi{दिन}} (\emph{dina}), from \textbf{Proto-Indo-Iranian} \emph{\textbf{*dinám}} — a \textbf{suffixed} formation built on \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*dyew-}} ("\textbf{to shine, sky}"), the same ultimate root behind \textbf{Latin}'s own \textbf{diēs}. But be careful: \emph{din} and \emph{diēs} aren't the closest possible cousins — they took \textbf{separate derivational paths} off that shared root. \emph{Din}'s own closest relatives are actually the Baltic/Slavic "day"-words, \textbf{Lithuanian} \emph{diena} and \textbf{Proto-Slavic} \emph{\textbf{*d\ru{ь}n\ru{ь}}}. The genuinely \textbf{direct}, unsuffixed cousins of \emph{diēs} are Sanskrit's own \textbf{\hi{द्यु}} (\emph{dyu}, "heaven, sky") and \textbf{\hi{दिव्}} (\emph{div}, "sky") — which give \textbf{\hi{दिवस}} (\emph{divasa}), yet another everyday Hindi word for "day." So the honest picture: \emph{din} and \emph{diēs} share one distant ancestor, but \emph{dyu}/\emph{div} are the tighter match.
